newsitem.title: INDONESIA: East Timor governor congratulates Belo on prize.
newsitem.headline: East Timor governor congratulates Belo on prize.

text.p: East Timor's joint Nobel Peace Prize winner Bishop Carlos Belo was congratulated for the award by the territory's Jakarta-appointed governor during a ceremonial mass for a new priest, a churchgoer said on Sunday.

Florentino Sarmento, who heads a rural development organisation, said Governor Abilio Soares, the vice-governor and the military and police commanders in the territory attended the mass and a luncheon that followed on Saturday.
Sarmento told Reuters by phone from the East Timor capital Dili that when the prize was announced at the church, "there was a lot of clapping of hands. Everyone was very proud".
"The governor on behalf of the government wished good luck and congratulations to the bishop during the ceremony," he said.
Belo, an outspoken Jesuit and probably the most influential individual in East Timor, has consistently championed the rights of the East Timorese and has intervened to halt violence.
The worst most recent incident was in 1991 when troops fired on protesters following a funeral procession, killing at least 50 people by official count.
The United Nations described it as a "massacre" and human rights groups put the death toll at around 200.
Sarmento and other sources said East Timor was quiet on Sunday, although there had been a tightening of security ahead of the scheduled visit to Dili by President Suharto on Tuesday.
The president is due to inaugurate several projects during a one-day trip to the former Portuguese colony which Jakarta invaded in December 1975 and annexed the following year.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee on Friday named Belo and Australia-based Timorese independence activist Ramos-Horta as joint recipients of the 1996 award.

Indonesia has condemned the award. Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said he was astounded Ramos-Horta had won and called him a "political adventurist". He had no comment on the outspoken and often fiery Belo.
A senior Asian diplomat said on Saturday Indonesian officials had expressed surprise and indignation over the awards. Belo might be acceptable, he said, but not Ramos-Horta.
Belo was quoted in an interview with the Moslem Republika newspaper on Sunday as saying he would have preferred not to get the award.

"Actually, it is better I had not received the prize. With this prize, my responsibilities are heavier. There is more work I must do, whereas I want to give more attention to serving my religious community."
He said he did not know yet whether he would go to Oslo to receive the award.
Sarmento said Ramos-Horta was not mentioned at the Saturday ceremony.
"I think that the East Timorese are aware of it, are proud of it, as well. But the political circumstances I think do not allow people to express freely their feelings," he said.
The official Antara news agency said Governor Soares had criticised the Nobel committee for putting Ramos-Horta on the same footing as Belo.

Asked what effect the awards might have on East Timor, Sarmento said: "I hope that this will attract more seriousness from the government of Indonesia, and Portugal and the international community to bring a political solution, a political settlement to the issue, one that can be accepted by all the parties."
